Las proposiciones del tema anterior decí: The propositions of the previous topic said whether something is true or false. This topic groups objects together, and discovers that the two things are the same: belonging to a set is a proposition being true. The connectives “and”, “or” and “not” from [[lg-proposiciones|logic]] turn into intersection, union and complement.
En el tema anterior aprendiste a decidir: In the previous topic you learned to decide whether a claim is true or false. Now we are going to do something that looks much more modest —grouping things together— and turns out to be more powerful. Notice that the question “is it true that 3 is odd?” and the question “is 3 in the pile of odd numbers?” are the same question written two ways. That coincidence is no accident: it is the bridge by which the logic of the previous topic turns into mathematics, and we are going to cross it in this one.
Un <strong>conjunto</strong> es una cole: A set is a well-determined collection of objects. The whole demand is in those two last words: given any object, it has to be clear whether it belongs or not, with no room for argument. “The large numbers” will not do, because nobody could say where the border is; “the numbers greater than a thousand” will, because of any number you can answer yes or no. Nothing else is required: no order, no quantity, no resemblance between the elements.
Cuesta creer cuánto se puede levantar co: It is hard to believe how much can be built with so little. In the late nineteenth century it was discovered that numbers, functions, space and practically any mathematical object can be defined as sets made of sets. We are not going to do that here, but it is worth knowing that the ground you will walk on for the whole course is made of this single idea.
Dos maneras de decir quién está dentro: Two ways of saying who is inside
Para dar un conjunto hay que dejar claro: To give a set you have to make clear who its elements are, and that can be done in two ways. The first is the obvious one: listing them one by one inside braces. The set is then said to be given by enumeration, and that is only practical when there are few of them: nobody is going to list the set of even numbers.
La segunda es no listar a nadie y dar en: The second is to list nobody and give instead the rule that its elements, and only its elements, satisfy. The set is then said to be given by comprehension, and to write it you need three symbols that you should be able to say, not just recognise:
Las <strong>llaves</strong> $\\{\\ \\}$: The braces $\{\ \}$ are read “the set of all”.
Los <strong>dos puntos</strong> $:$ se l: The colon $:$ is read “such that”. In some books you will see a bar $|$ instead; it means the same.
El símbolo $\\in$ se lee «pertenece a»,: The symbol $\in$ is read “belongs to”, and the hollow letter $\mathbb{N}$ is said “N” and is the name of the natural numbers: $0, 1, 2, 3, \dots$
el mismo conjunto, por extensión y por c: the same set, by enumeration and by comprehension
La primera línea se dice: <em>«A es el c:
The first line is said: “A is the set made up of 1, 2, 3 and 4”.

The second, whole and without stopping: “A is the set of all x belonging to the natural numbers, such that x is less than 5 and x is different from zero”.

Symbol by symbol: $\{$ “the set of all” · $x$ “x” · $\in$ “belongs to” · $\mathbb{N}$ “N, the naturals” · $:$ “such that” · $\ne$ “different from”.
Las dos líneas describen el mismo conjun: The two lines describe the same set, and that is the point: the top one shows it and the bottom one describes it. If you are unsure how something is pronounced, press the ? in the corner of the box; you will find it on the new formulas throughout the course. It is worth reading it aloud once, because this way of writing will be with you until the last topic.
Con la idea de conjunto vienen cuatro sí: With the idea of a set come four symbols worth keeping fresh. The first three are relations —they say how something stands with respect to a set— and the fourth is a very particular set:
$x \\in A$: el elemento $x$ <strong>pert: $x \in A$: the element $x$ belongs to $A$. It is the basic question every set has to be able to answer.
$A \\subset B$: todo elemento de $A$ est: $A \subset B$: every element of $A$ is also in $B$; $A$ is said to be a subset of $B$. Careful, this is not about one element but about two whole sets.
$\\emptyset$: el conjunto <strong>vacío<: $\emptyset$: the empty set, the one with no elements at all. It looks useless and it is not: it is a subset of every set, and it will turn up whenever two things have nothing in common.
No importa el orden ni repetir un elemen: Order does not matter, and neither does repeating an element: $\{1,2,2,3\}$ and $\{3,1,2\}$ are the same set. A set only knows who is in it, not how many times nor in what order.
Cuidado con dos símbolos que se confunde: Beware of two symbols that get confused: $\in$ relates an element to a set, and $\subset$ relates two sets. If $A=\{1,2\}$, then $1 \in A$ and $\{1\} \subset A$, but $1 \subset A$ means nothing.
Sea $A = \\{2, 4, 6\\}$. ¿Cuál de estas: Let $A = \{2, 4, 6\}$. Which of these three sentences is correctly written and true?
El 4 es un elemento, y $\\in$ es justo l: 4 is an element, and $\in$ is precisely the relation between an element and a set.
$\\subset$ compara dos conjuntos, y el 4: $\subset$ compares two sets, and 4 is not a set: the sentence means nothing.
$\\{4\\}$ es un conjunto de un elemento,: $\{4\}$ is a set with one element, and $A$ does not contain sets, it contains numbers. The correct statement would be $\{4\} \subset A$.
Con dos números puedes hacer cosas: suma: With two numbers you can do things: add them, subtract them, multiply them. With two sets you can too, and the operations that exist are not an arbitrary invention: they come from asking the only thing a set can answer. If I have two sets $A$ and $B$ and pick any object, there are four possible answers —it is in both, only in $A$, only in $B$, or in neither— and each operation is nothing more than keeping some of those four regions.
De ahí salen las cinco de la tabla. Léel: That is where the five in the table come from. Read it slowly, paying attention to the last column, because the surprise of the topic is hidden there: every operation is defined with one of the words you were using yesterday to talk about true and false.
Es el conjunto de los que…: It is the set of those that…
Compara esta tabla con la de las conecti: Compare this table with the one for the connectives in the previous topic. Union is the “or”, intersection is the “and”, complement is the “not”. Sets are logic drawn: that is why De Morgan works here just the same.
La rayita de encima se lee «complementar:
The little bar on top is read “complement of”, or more plainly “everything that is NOT in”. So the first line is said: “the complement of A intersection B equals the complement of A union the complement of B”.

In plain words: “what is not in both at once is the same as what is missing from one or missing from the other”.

The two symbols: $\cap$ is said “intersection” (the common region) and $\cup$ is said “union” (everything together).
Elige una operación y mira qué región qu: Pick an operation and look at which region is shaded. Compare the last pair: they are the same region, and that is De Morgan.
Antes de pulsar $\\overline{A \\cap B}$:: Before pressing $\overline{A \cap B}$: which part of the picture do you think will be shaded, a lot or a little? Will it match the one for $\overline{A} \cup \overline{B}$?
Toda base de datos del mundo funciona co: Every database in the world works with these operations, and even with these names: UNION, INTERSECT, EXCEPT. When a hospital crosses “patients with this condition” with “patients taking this drug”, it is doing an intersection; when a shop looks for whoever bought last year but not this one, a difference. The Venn diagram you draw here is literally what the server executes.
Hasta ahora hemos hablado de <em>quién</: So far we have talked about who is in a set. Now we are going to ask how many, which is a different question and a tricky one. The cardinality of $A$, written $|A|$, is simply its number of elements.
Contar un conjunto solo es fácil hasta q: Counting one set is easy only until a second one appears. Imagine a class of 30 students where 18 play football and 15 play basketball. How many do sport? The temptation is to say 33, which is also impossible because there are only 30. The error is that anyone who plays both has been counted twice, once in each group, so they have to be discounted once:
Las barras verticales se leen «cardinal:
The vertical bars are read “cardinality of”, which is the short way of saying “how many elements it has”.

Whole: “the cardinality of A union B equals the cardinality of A, plus the cardinality of B, minus the cardinality of A intersection B”.

Said the way you think it: “those in A or in B are those in A plus those in B, taking away once those that were in both”.
Con 18 y 15 sobre 30, el número de repet: With 18 and 15 out of 30, the number of duplicates is $18+15-30=3$. Keep this idea of adding and discounting the overlap: it will reappear exactly as it is when you compute the probability that one thing or the other happens.
En otra clase, 12 alumnos tocan un instr: In another class, 12 students play an instrument, 9 sing in the choir and 4 do both. How many do at least one of the two?
Has sumado sin más: los 4 que hacen las: You just added: the 4 who do both are counted twice.
Has descontado los 4 dos veces. Solo est: You discounted the 4 twice. They were only counted once too often.
Combinar dos conjuntos en lugar de mezcl: Combining two sets instead of mixing them
La unión y la intersección meten los ele: Union and intersection put the elements of $A$ and $B$ into the same bag. There is another way of joining them that does not mix them: pairing them up. If $A$ is the sizes of a T-shirt and $B$ the colours, what interests the shop is not the union of the two but the list of combinations —size M in blue, size L in blue, size M in red…— which is a new object.
Ese objeto es el <strong>producto cartes: That object is the Cartesian product $A \times B$: the set of all ordered pairs with the first element from $A$ and the second from $B$. Here, unlike what happened inside a set, order does matter: $(1,2)$ and $(2,1)$ are different pairs, just as “size M in red” is not “size red in M”.
Contarlos es inmediato: por cada elecció: Counting them is immediate: for each choice of the first there are as many possibilities as the second set has elements, so they multiply.
Se lee: <em>«el cardinal de A por B es i:
It is read: “the cardinality of A times B equals the cardinality of A multiplied by the cardinality of B”.

Careful with the cross: between two sets, $\times$ is not a multiplication but the “Cartesian product”, the list of all possible pairs. What does get multiplied is the quantities, which is what the right-hand side says.
$\\mathbb{R} \\times \\mathbb{R} = \\mat: $\mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R} = \mathbb{R}^2$ is the plane. Every point of the plane is an ordered pair of reals. All the analytic geometry you have studied rests on this definition.
Llegamos a la idea más productiva del te: We come to the most productive idea of the topic. Until now sets have been piles sitting still; now we are going to relate them, and that is what a map (or function) $f: A \to B$ is for: a rule that assigns to each element of $A$ exactly one element of $B$. $A$ is called the domain and $B$ the codomain.
Las dos palabras que hacen todo el traba: The two phrases that do all the work are “to each” and “exactly one”. The first forbids leaving anybody unassigned: if a single element of $A$ is left without a destination, there is no map. The second forbids ambiguity: an element of $A$ cannot go to two places at once. Think of a gym changing room —each member has their locker assigned, one and only one—; whereas “a person's telephone number” will not do as a map, because some people have two and some have none.
Fíjate en que la definición no dice nada: Notice that the definition says nothing about $B$. It is perfectly legal for two members to share a locker, or for lockers to be left empty: what is demanded is about who leaves, not about who receives. And precisely for that reason, asking what happens in $B$ is what gives rise to the classification that follows.
Hay dos cosas que pueden estropearse en: There are two things that can go wrong in $B$: somebody receiving two arrows, or somebody receiving none. Forbidding the first gives the injective maps, forbidding the second the surjective ones, and forbidding both at once, the bijective ones:
elementos distintos van a imágenes disti: different elements go to different images: nobody shares a destination
no sobra ningún elemento en el conjunto: no element is left over in the codomain: everybody receives something
emparejamiento perfecto, uno a uno: a perfect pairing, one to one
Si $A$ tiene 3 elementos y $B$ tiene 2,: If $A$ has 3 elements and $B$ has 2, can there be an injective map from $A$ to $B$? And a surjective one? Decide before looking at the arrows.
Cada flecha lleva un elemento de A a uno: Each arrow takes an element of A to one of B. Look at whether there are shared destinations (not injective) or empty destinations (not surjective).
Clasificar la misma fórmula con tres con: Classifying the same formula with three codomains
La regla $f(x) = x^2$ se puede plantear: The rule $f(x) = x^2$ can be set up between different sets, and the classification changes even though the formula does not. We are going to look at $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$, $f:\mathbb{R}\to[0,+\infty)$ and $f:[0,+\infty)\to[0,+\infty)$.
<strong>Inyectiva?</strong> Buscamos dos: Injective? We look for two different inputs with the same image. $f(2) = f(-2) = 4$: there are some. With $\mathbb{R}$ as the domain, it is not injective.
¿Se te ocurren dos números distintos con: Can you think of two different numbers with the same square?
<strong>Sobreyectiva?</strong> Con conju: Surjective? With codomain $\mathbb{R}$, does any $x$ satisfy $x^2 = -1$? No: the negatives are left without a source. $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ is neither injective nor surjective.
¿Hay algún número real cuyo cuadrado sea: Is there any real number whose square is $-1$?
Si el conjunto final es $[0,+\\infty)$,: If the codomain is $[0,+\infty)$, nobody is left over any more: every $y \ge 0$ is $(\sqrt{y})^2$. $f:\mathbb{R}\to[0,+\infty)$ is surjective, but it is still not injective because of step 1.
Si solo se permiten imágenes no negativa: If only non-negative images are allowed, is any destination still left over?
Si además el conjunto inicial es $[0,+\\: If the domain is also $[0,+\infty)$, the $-2$ of step 1 disappears: two different non-negative numbers have different squares. $f:[0,+\infty)\to[0,+\infty)$ is bijective, and its inverse is the square root.
Si quitamos los negativos del conjunto i: If we remove the negatives from the domain, can there still be two inputs with the same image?
Moraleja: una aplicación no es solo una: Moral: a map is not just a formula, it is a formula between two sets. Changing the sets changes the classification.
Las <strong>biyecciones</strong> van a s: Bijections are going to be hugely important later on: they are the tool with which Cantor compared the sizes of infinite sets. If a bijection exists between two sets, “they have the same elements”, even if they are infinite.
La teoría de conjuntos la creó Georg Can: Set theory was created by Georg Cantor between 1874 and 1897, and it was received with hostility: Kronecker called it “mathematical charlatanry”. In 1901 Russell found a devastating paradox in its naive version: if we consider “the set of all sets that do not contain themselves”, does it contain itself? Either answer leads to a contradiction. The theory had to be rebuilt with more careful axioms, and out of that crisis came modern mathematical logic.
$3 \\in \\{1, 3\\}$, pero $\\{3\\} \\sub: $3 \in \{1, 3\}$, but $\{3\} \subset \{1, 3\}$: the element belongs, the set is included. And $\varnothing \subset A$ always, even though it does not belong.
El complementario de $A \\cap B$ es $\\o: The complement of $A \cap B$ is $\overline{A} \cup \overline{B}$: intersection turns into union. With a Venn diagram you see it in a second.
Con $|A| = 5$, $|B| = 4$ y dos elementos: With $|A| = 5$, $|B| = 4$ and two common elements, $|A \cup B| = 5 + 4 - 2 = 7$. Adding without subtracting counts the common ones twice.
Cada elemento de $A$ tiene que tener exa: Every element of $A$ has to have exactly one image. One with no arrow, or with two, is not a map however much the picture may look like one.
Una aplicación aparece en un sitio donde: A map turns up in a place where almost nobody looks for it: inside any running program. What an interpreter consults when it meets a variable name is exactly a map $E$ from a set of names into the set of values. Declaring is adding a pair, assigning is changing an image, and using the name is evaluating $E(x)$. It is developed in [[len-variables|the machines and languages block]], and from there, with no further theory, comes the reason why a name cannot mean two things at once.
Que una aplicación sea inyectiva es lo q: A map being injective is what makes an identifier useful: if two people could have the same ID number, the ID number would identify nobody. Being bijective is what makes something undoable: compressing a file and getting it back intact, encrypting a message and decrypting it. And functions that deliberately are not injective work too: when a website stores your password as a digest, it uses a function that crushes any text into a fixed code, precisely so that it cannot be reversed.
La intersección son los que están en los: The intersection is those that are in both.
The union is all of them, without repeating.
Los de $A$ quitando los que también esté: Those in $A$ minus the ones that are also in $B$.
Those in the universe that are not in $A$.
Recorremos los elementos aplicando la de: We go through the elements applying the definition of the operation.

$, ¿cuántos elementos tiene $A \\times B: $, how many elements does $A \times B$ have?

Cada par se forma eligiendo un elemento: Each pair is formed by choosing an element of $A$ and one of $B$: the multiplication principle.
Para cada elemento hay dos opciones: ent: For each element there are two options: it goes into the subset or it does not.
Cada par ordenado se construye eligiendo: Each ordered pair is built by choosing first an element of $A$ and then one of $B$.
Para construir un subconjunto, se decide: To build a subset, you decide for each element whether it goes in or not: two options each.
